claims.text: A central Army special-access oversight office predates the 1994 reform by ten years. GAO/NSIAD-88-152 records: 'A DOD review of Army special access programs in 1983 revealed systemic weaknesses in various management areas, which resulted in establishment of a central oversight office in September 1984.' The same report states that in 1988 'The Deputy Under Secretary of Defense for Policy is required to maintain a listing of all special access programs, but does not do so because of security concerns', and that 'the Secretary's Office has no centralized office with cognizance of all special access programs'. The January 1994 dates this board carries stand; the Army aftermath began in 1983-84.

claims.source: Deputy Secretary of Defense, Special Access Program Oversight Committee, Information Bulletin, November 1994, as transcribed at https://sgp.fas.org/othergov/sapoc.html
claims.text: The committee was established on 5 January 1994, sixteen years before the directive this node cites. A Deputy Secretary of Defense information bulletin of November 1994 states: 'On January 5th, 1994, the Deputy Secretary of Defense (DEPSECDEF) significantly enhanced changes in the DoD Special Access Program (SAP) management and control structures. ... The plan standardized and formalized the SAP approval, termination, revalidation and restructuring process through the Special Access Program Oversight Committee (SAPOC). A Senior Review Group (SRG) was established to support the SAPOC principals.' Tier 2 because the text opened is a transcription published by the Federation of American Scientists and no scan of the original bulletin was found from this environment.

claims.text: The annual review and validation function this node attributes to the 2010 directive is in the 1994 bulletin: 'All SAPs will be reviewed and validated annually for continued SAP status by the OSD SAPOC. ... The DEPSECDEF is the final decision maker in establishing, disestablishing or restructuring SAPs.'

claims.source: Deputy Secretary of Defense, SAPOC Information Bulletin, November 1994, https://sgp.fas.org/othergov/sapoc.html
claims.text: The 1994 membership was five principals and an executive secretary, not the roughly eighteen of the later instruction: 'The SAPOC is chaired by the Honorable John Deutch, DEPSECDEF, with permanent members the Honorable Paul Kaminski USD(A&T), the Honorable Walter Slocombe USD(P), ADM William A. Owens, VCJCS, and the Honorable Emmett Paige Jr., ASD(C3I). BGEN Mike Kostelnik, OUSD(A&T), serves as both member and executive secretary to the SAPOC in his capacity as director of the SAPCO (SAP Coordinating Office). SAPOC membership is not further delegable.' The node's argument about a large in-house validating body describes the later era, not this one.

claims.source: Joint Security Commission, Redefining Security: A Report to the Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence, 28 February 1994, chapter 2, https://sgp.fas.org/library/jsc/chap2.html
claims.text: A commission chartered by the Secretary of Defense and the Director of Central Intelligence corroborated the formation within two months: 'Until recently there has been no procedure for centralized assessment of special program proposals submitted directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense by the military departments. The recent formation of the DoD Special Access Program Oversight Committee, which the Commission fully supports, will ensure that every program is reviewed by a panel of senior officials prior to its establishment, and annually thereafter, to determine whether compartmentation for each program is still required.'

DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.b: 'The Special Access Program Oversight Committee (SAPOC), hereby established, shall advise and assist the Secretary of Defense (SecDef) and the Deputy Secretary of Defense with governance, management, and oversight of DoD SAPs, as provided in Enclosure 2.'

DoDD 5205.07 (2024) retains the SAPOC as the 'senior governing body' ensuring SAPs 'meet warfighter needs while protecting CPI', chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense with the Director, DoD SAPCO as Executive Secretary.

DoDI 5205.11 para 3.5.a.(3): the SAPOC shall 'Conduct an annual review of DoD SAPs to assess the continuing need for protection of CPI within SAP security controls, in accordance with E.O. 13526 and DoDD 5205.07', and para 3.5.a.(3)(d) extends that review to 'All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status.'

DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.b: 'The Special Access Program Oversight Committee (SAPOC), hereby established, shall advise and assist the Secretary of Defense (SecDef) and the Deputy Secretary of Defense with governance, management, and oversight of DoD SAPs.'

DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3: SAPOC membership is Chair - the Deputy Secretary of Defense; Vice-Chair - USD(AT&L); Executive Secretary - Director, DoD SAPCO; with general membership USD(P), USD(C)/CFO, USD(I), USD(P&R), the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, DoD CIO, GC DoD, DCAPE, the Under Secretaries of the Army, Navy and Air Force, the Vice Chiefs of Staff of the Army and Air Force, the Vice Chief of Naval Operations and the Assistant Commandant of the Marine Corps.

DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 para 2.b(3): the SAPOC convenes at the direction of the Deputy Secretary of Defense to 'Conduct an annual review and validation of SAP reports sent to the Congressional defense and intelligence committees.'

DoDD 5205.07 (12 September 2024) retains the SAPOC as 'the senior governing body of the DoD SAP Enterprise for governance, management, and oversight of DoD SAPs', chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense.

Because the SAPOC both validates the congressional SAP report and sits under the official who approves carve-outs and waivers, the Department's account of its own special access programs is produced entirely inside the compartment it describes, with no external validator at any point. Reasoning: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 gives the annual validation to the SAPOC and no issuance assigns any external body a concurrent validation role.

desc: The SAPOC was established on 5 January 1994, not in 2010. A Deputy Secretary of Defense information bulletin of November 1994 records that 'On January 5th, 1994, the Deputy Secretary of Defense (DEPSECDEF) significantly enhanced changes in the DoD Special Access Program (SAP) management and control structures' and that the plan 'standardized and formalized the SAP approval, termination, revalidation and restructuring process through the Special Access Program Oversight Committee (SAPOC). A Senior Review Group (SRG) was established to support the SAPOC principals'; the Joint Security Commission called it a 'recent formation' on 28 February 1994. DoD Directive 5205.07 of 1 July 2010 is therefore a later instrument that re-established a committee which had been running for sixteen years, and it survives in the 12 September 2024 reissue as 'the senior governing body of the DoD SAP Enterprise'. Under the 2013 instruction its chair is the Deputy Secretary of Defense, its vice-chair the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology and Logistics, and its executive secretary the Director of DoD SAPCO; its general membership is the Under Secretaries for Policy, Comptroller/CFO, Intelligence, and Personnel and Readiness, the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the DoD Chief Information Officer, the General Counsel of the Department, the Director of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation, the Under Secretaries of the Army, Navy and Air Force, the Vice Chiefs of Staff of the Army and Air Force, the Vice Chief of Naval Operations and the Assistant Commandant of the Marine Corps. Its three primary functions are to review issues on which the Senior Review Group could not reach unanimity, to ensure combatant command warfighting needs are reflected in SAP programmatics and budgets, and - the function that matters here - to 'Conduct an annual review and validation of SAP reports sent to the Congressional defense and intelligence committees'. In other words, the document Congress receives about special access programs is written and validated by a committee of roughly eighteen senior officials of the Department the report is about, chaired by the same official who signs the carve-outs. This is the body whose membership a witness alleging concealment would have to say was either complicit or itself deceived; DoD's own directive makes that a binary with no third option.
